### 3. What a "session" is

A heartbeat record says that an avatar was online at one poll. It does not say
when the player logged in, when they logged out, or how many separate sittings
the month contained. Building that from the polls is what `skrub.SessionEncoder`
does, and the result is the raw material for the session features.

#### The rule

A session is a run of heartbeats in which consecutive beats are at most
`session_gap` apart. One character's beats are sorted by time, the gap to the
previous beat is computed, and every gap larger than the threshold opens a new
session:

```python
session_encoder = SessionEncoder(
    split_by="char", timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap * 60
)
beats = session_encoder.fit_transform(month_of_heartbeats)
```

The encoder is stateless and it only *adds* a column (`timestamp_session_id`):
every row, and its original order, comes back untouched. That is what makes it
usable inside the feature function instead of as a pre-processing step, and it is
also why it has to be refit for each month — sessions are a property of the data
being encoded, not a fixed transformation.

#### The gap is a choice, not a constant

Polls arrive roughly every ten minutes, so a gap of ten minutes means nothing
and a gap of a few hours means the player left. Where to put the boundary is a
modelling decision, and it is small enough to tune: `session_gap` is declared as
a skrub choice and searched along with everything else.

```python
session_gap = skrub.choose_from([30, 60, 15], name="session_gap")
```

On the 2008 data, 83.6% of consecutive-heartbeat gaps are within 15 minutes,
89.8% within 30 and 91.0% within 60, so the three candidates sit in the flat part
of the distribution rather than cutting through the mass of one-poll gaps. Their
effect on the features is real but not dramatic: over March 2008 a character-month
has a median of 4 sessions at any of the three gaps, and the mean falls from 15.2
at 15 minutes to 12.0 at 60.

Because it is a choice rather than a constant, the search tunes the definition of
a session exactly like it tunes the learning rate — the boundary of the
"behaviour" the model sees is part of the search space.

#### What one night looks like

Character 66560 on 2008-03-14, with `session_gap = 30` minutes. The 50m 14s gap
crosses the threshold and opens a second session; the 20m 18s gap does not:

| beat | gap to previous | session |
|--------|-----------|:-----:|
| 21:51:06 | — | 0 |
| 22:00:50 | 9m 44s | 0 |
| 22:11:23 | 10m 33s | 0 |
| 22:21:07 | 9m 44s | 0 |
| 23:11:21 | 50m 14s | 1 |
| 23:21:04 | 9m 43s | 1 |
| 23:41:22 | 20m 18s | 1 |
| 23:51:05 | 9m 43s | 1 |

The same heartbeats at 15 and 60 minutes give three sessions and one session
respectively:

![](images/session_gap_example.png){fig-align="center"}

#### From sessions to one row per month

Sessions are only an intermediate: the model consumes one row per
(character, month), so the sessions are collapsed by `add_session_features`.
Character 66560 has 9 sessions in March 2008:

| session | start | end | duration |
|:--:|-----------|-----------|------|
| 0 | 03-01 09:08 | 03-01 11:38 | 2h 30m |
| 1 | 03-01 22:28 | 03-01 22:28 | 1m |
| 2 | 03-05 21:41 | 03-05 22:21 | 39m 45s |
| 3 | 03-08 10:40 | 03-08 11:31 | 50m 14s |
| 4 | 03-09 08:41 | 03-09 11:31 | 2h 50m |
| 5 | 03-09 12:11 | 03-09 13:41 | 1h 30m |
| 6 | 03-14 21:51 | 03-14 22:21 | 30m 01s |
| 7 | 03-14 23:11 | 03-14 23:51 | 39m 44s |
| 8 | 03-15 11:11 | 03-15 11:41 | 29m 57s |

which become the features attached to that character's **April** row:

| feature | value |
|----------------------------------|-----------|
| `monthly_num_sessions` | 9 |
| `monthly_total_session_duration` | 10h 01m |
| `monthly_avg_session_duration` | 1h 07m |
| `monthly_std_session_duration` | 58m 02s |
| `monthly_avg_session_start` | 02:20 |
| `monthly_avg_session_end` | 03:27 |

Two details are worth spelling out. Session 1 is a single heartbeat, so its
measured duration would be zero; `get_session_duration` gives it one minute
instead, so that "logged in briefly" stays distinguishable from "never logged
in". And the standard deviation is computed on microseconds rather than on the
`Duration` column, because polars cannot take the std of a duration directly.

#### A second sessionisation, for locations

The same encoder runs again with `split_by=["char", "zone"]`, producing
`timestamp_session_id_zone`. Those sessions measure how long a character stayed
in a given zone, not how long they played, and they are what the location
features are built on: time spent per zone, how much of it lands in "hub" zones
that everyone visits, and how evenly it is spread. It is a separate pass with a
separate column, so the two sessionisations never interfere.

```python
session_encoder_zone = SessionEncoder(
    split_by=["char", "zone"],
    timestamp_col="timestamp",
    session_gap=session_gap * 60,
    suffix="session_id_zone",
)
```
